figures.caption: Fig. 5. Per-segment dynamics by (task, scaler): executed joint speed, executed joint acceleration, and approach pitch. Six tasks × three scalers: Mode B (yellow), Interpolated (green), Mode A (blue); hatched cells are the two motion-mode transfer conditions (push at Mode A, highfive at Mode B). Every metric separates Mode A from Mode B on trained tasks, with the intermediate scaler falling between.

Fig. 6. Quantized latents zqsp (top) and zqte (bottom), projected via PCA; colored by task (left) and scaler s (right). Spatial codes cluster by task and are interleaved across modes; temporal codes form a clean Mode B / Mode A band and overlap across tasks. The Stage 1 decomposition is preserved at deployment.

Fig. 2. Mode A vs. Mode B on real rollouts, illustrating why each suits different manipulation contexts. Mode A (steady): slow, precise motion that holds a constant end-effector orientation, suited to secure transfer of delicate items. Mode B (dynamic): faster, more tolerant pacing with dynamic orientation changes (e.g., facing the user), suited to interactiondriven handling.

Fig. 8. Subjective Likert evaluation across six tasks × three scalers. Left: mean style adhesion, monotonic in the requested scaler on every task, including the two motion-mode transfer cells (hatched). Right: mean task completion (0 = complete failure, 10 = fully successful). Color: Mode B yellow, Interpolated green, Mode A blue. Error bars: SEM across raters/rollouts.

Fig. 3. MoMo training overview. (a) Stage 1: spatial (1D-conv) and temporal (DCT+MLP) encoders, each quantized by an independent RVQ stack and recombined via a Fusion module into a shared decoder; trained with reconstruction, DCT, disentanglement (adversarial MI + contrastive), and swap losses. (b) Stage 2: a transformer predicts code indices from images, proprioception, task, and motion mode (cross-entropy loss) over the frozen Stage-1 codebooks; a continuous offset head corrects the decoder output (L1 loss).
